reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases
clinicalPearls: An acquired paraneoplastic syndrome in which a usually small, benign mesenchymal tumour secretes fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), driving renal phosphate wasting
Typically presents in adults with insidious bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and recurrent fragility fractures often misattributed to other rheumatological disease
Biochemistry shows hypophosphataemia with inappropriate phosphaturia and a low or inappropriately normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D despite the low phosphate
Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone are usually normal, and alkaline phosphatase is commonly raised reflecting osteomalacia
The culprit phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour is often tiny and occult, hiding in the extremities, craniofacial region, or acral soft tissue and bone
Functional imaging exploiting somatostatin-receptor expression, alongside FGF23-guided venous sampling, aids localisation of an elusive tumour
Complete surgical resection is curative and normalises phosphate; when the tumour cannot be found or removed, phosphate salts with active vitamin D or FGF23-directed antibody therapy are used
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours ectopically overproduce FGF23 (and related phosphatonins). Circulating FGF23 acts on the proximal renal tubule to downregulate sodium-phosphate cotransporters, causing renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia. FGF23 also suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase and stimulates 24-hydroxylase, so 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is inappropriately low or normal for the degree of hypophosphataemia, limiting compensatory intestinal phosphate absorption. Chronic hypophosphataemia impairs mineralisation of osteoid, producing osteomalacia with bone pain, weakness, and fractures. Because the mechanism mirrors the inherited FGF23-driven rickets syndromes, the biochemical fingerprint is shared, but here it is acquired and reversible with tumour removal.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets and other inherited FGF23-mediated phosphate-wasting disorders
Nutritional or malabsorptive vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia
Fanconi syndrome with generalised proximal tubulopathy
Primary hyperparathyroidism and other metabolic bone disease
Polymyalgia rheumatica or inflammatory myopathy given the proximal weakness
Metastatic bone disease or multiple myeloma
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum phosphate with paired urine studies (tubular reabsorption of phosphate / TmP-GFR) to confirm renal phosphate wasting
Serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, alkaline phosphatase, and 25- and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D metabolites
Measurement of intact FGF23, which is elevated or inappropriately normal
Functional somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g. gallium-labelled DOTA-peptide PET) to localise the occult tumour
Cross-sectional anatomical imaging of suspicious sites and selective venous sampling for FGF23 when localisation is difficult
Histological confirmation of a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour after resection
redFlags: Recurrent low-trauma fractures with unexplained persistent hypophosphataemia
Progressive proximal weakness leading to falls and immobility
Failure of symptoms to resolve after apparent resection, suggesting incomplete removal or malignant behaviour
Nephrocalcinosis or hypercalciuria complicating high-dose phosphate and active vitamin D therapy
reference.prognosis: Complete resection of the responsible tumour is curative, with rapid normalisation of phosphate and gradual healing of osteomalacia; when the tumour is unresectable or occult, long-term medical therapy controls symptoms but requires monitoring for secondary hyperparathyroidism and nephrocalcinosis.
pitfalls: Overlooking hypophosphataemia because routine panels omit phosphate or the low value is dismissed as artefact
Attributing symptoms to primary rheumatological or psychiatric illness, delaying diagnosis for years
Abandoning the search for an occult tumour before functional and venous sampling techniques are exhausted
Inducing tertiary hyperparathyroidism and renal calcinosis with unmonitored phosphate and calcitriol supplementation
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
management: Complete surgical resection of the culprit phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour, which is curative and rapidly normalises phosphate
Oral phosphate supplementation combined with active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol) when the tumour is occult or unresectable
The anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody burosumab as targeted medical therapy where conventional replacement is inadequate
Functional somatostatin-receptor imaging with anatomical imaging and selective venous FGF23 sampling to localise the elusive tumour
Ablative approaches such as radiofrequency ablation for tumours not amenable to surgical resection
Surveillance for the complications of medical therapy, namely secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism and nephrocalcinosis
Multidisciplinary metabolic bone, surgical and radiology input
